title: Three run silently, one stops
spec: CC4 · allow / ask / deny on the PublicRecords API
intro: Four requests that all look like "run a Maven command". Three of them never interrupt you. The fourth stops the session dead and waits. The only thing that changed is a file you wrote once and committed.

provenance.source: a narrated session against the shipped labs/cc/PublicRecordsAPI project; commands and file paths are real, terminal output is reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: labs/cc/PublicRecordsAPI — CC4 lab, steps 2–5.

steps.title: Write the rules once, commit them
narrative: Permissions live in .claude/settings.json at the project root, which means they are reviewable in a pull request and identical for everyone on the team. Three lists stack: allow runs silently, ask prompts you, deny refuses with no prompt offered.

The matcher syntax is prefix-plus-wildcard: Bash(mvn test:*) matches any Bash invocation starting mvn test. Drop the trailing :* and you match the bare command only — which is the single most common reason a rule you "definitely wrote" still prompts you.
steps.youDo: mkdir -p .claude, write the file below, then git add .claude/settings.json && git commit -m "chore(claude): project permission tiers".

terminal.text:
Model:    claude-sonnet-4-5
Mode:     default
Settings: User (~/.claude/settings.json)
          Project (.claude/settings.json)  ← 10 allow · 6 ask · 8 deny

before.title: BEFORE — nothing configured, every Bash call prompts

view.note: With empty lists you approve mvn test by hand every single time — which is exactly how people end up reaching for a blanket bypass instead.

after.title: AFTER — the tiers the lab ships

view.note: The dividing line is not "how dangerous does it sound" — it is who sees it. Everything in allow is invisible outside your machine. Everything in ask is visible to the team or to production.

steps.title: Three requests, no prompts
narrative: Run the inner loop. Tests, then a compile-only pass, then the working tree — three separate tool calls, three matches against allow, zero interruptions.

The seed data makes the assertions concrete: data.sql loads 8 filings across 6 states, and FilingControllerTest pins exactly that — 8 rows on /filings, 2 on ?state=TX, 404 on an unknown id. If a rule is too narrow you find out here, because a prompt appears where none should.
steps.youDo: Run the tests. Now compile only — don't run tests this time. Show me git status.

steps.title: The fourth one stops
narrative: Same shape of request, same three words of preamble, same mvn binary. This one publishes an artifact to a repository other people pull from — so it is in ask, and the session halts until you answer.

Read the three options. "Yes, and don't ask again" writes the rule into .claude/settings.local.json for you, which is convenient and is also how an ask tier quietly becomes an allow tier over a few weeks. Pick it deliberately or not at all.
steps.youDo: Run mvn deploy to push this to staging. Then answer No — nothing should actually deploy.

terminal.text: Run `mvn deploy` to push this to staging.
Bash  mvn deploy         ask ← Bash(mvn deploy:*)

Bash command
  mvn deploy
  Publish publicrecords-api:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT to the staging repository

Do you want to proceed?
  1. Yes
  2. Yes, and don't ask again for mvn deploy commands in this project
  3. No, and tell Claude what to do differently (esc)
› 3   permission denied by user — command not run

Understood, I won't deploy. The build is green locally if you want to
release it yourself, or I can open a PR instead.

before.title: BEFORE — the request, indistinguishable from the other three

view.text: mvn deploy reads as one more Maven goal in a session that just ran three of them without comment. Nothing in the phrasing marks it as different.

after.title: AFTER — the rule that caught it

view.note: ask is not deny: the call was stoppable, and you stopped it. A deny rule like Bash(mvn flyway:clean:*) would not have offered you the choice at all.

steps.title: What the allow-list is not
narrative: Four requests, one file, one interruption — that is the win, and it is a real one: the cost of a permission prompt is not the click, it is that you stop reading and start clicking, and then blanket-bypass everything because the prompts got noisy.

But be clear about what you bought. Permissions match the command string, not what the command does. Bash(mvn spring-boot:run:*) is pre-approved, and a Maven plugin declared in pom.xml can do anything the JVM can do — including reach the network. Edit(src/**) lets Claude write whatever it likes inside src/. The allow-list stops the wrong verb; it does not sandbox the right one.

That is the seam the lab's step 7 fills with a sandbox profile, where the OS — not a matcher — blocks writes outside the project root and traffic to non-allowlisted domains. Use permissions for intent, the sandbox for consequence.

view.text: A rule that fires is only as good as the rule you wrote. Bash(mvn deploy) without the trailing :* would have missed mvn deploy -DskipTests entirely — and you would never have known, because a rule that matches nothing produces no output. Prove each tier the way this lab does: run one command per tier and check that the right thing happened, not just that something did.
